competitors.name: PackPoint / PackPoint Premium
competitors.model: Free with ads on Android; one-time unlocks rather than a subscription — Premium Package $2.99, 'Manage default activities and list items' $0.99, TripIt Integration $0.99 (iOS App Store IAP list). Separate paid 'PackPoint Premium' SKU also exists.
competitors.note: The category default and the app everyone benchmarks against: 4.7 from ~2,400 iOS ratings, ~4.0 from ~40,600 Android reviews. Its whole pitch is the thing we do not do — it takes a destination city, dates and activities and generates the list from a live weather forecast. Three exploitable soft spots, all documented in its own reviews. (1) The list is assembled in the cloud, so you need a connection to create one (journeybot's 2026 comparison) — it is weakest in an airport, on a plane, or abroad without data, which is exactly when a packing list gets opened. (2) It is single-traveller only: 'PackPoint only creates packing lists for one person and you can't add travelers' (TooManyAdapters). (3) Nothing is editable after creation — city and dates can only be deleted and recreated. Also visibly under-maintained: a 2-star review from 05/02/2024 complains 'It has not been updated in 7 months!'

competitors.name: Packr / Packr Premium
competitors.model: Free tier (unlimited trips/items, 3-day forecast) plus an unusually long IAP ladder on iOS: $0.99 'Premium promo', $1.99 'Premium special offer', $2.99 one month, $4.99, $5.99, $19.99 'Premium access', $49.99 'Packr Premium'. Third-party trackers also list $3.49/mo, $24.99/yr and $34.99 lifetime.
competitors.note: The design leader — 4.6 from ~7,000 iOS ratings, and the app reviewers describe as having 'modern colors, icons, and design' (4-star, sfmichelle, 04/13/2018). It is also the clearest example of a free tool tightening the screws: aggregated review analysis flags 'aggressive paywall transitions force users to pay for basic functionality that was previously free', attraction-based ads that obstruct the packing workflow, and data loss after a recent update. Family mode — the single most requested feature in the category — is premium-only, and it asks you to sign in with your Apple account before trips will save and sync. Ten different price points for a checklist is itself the argument for our position.

competitors.name: PackGoat
competitors.model: Free tier; Pro at $3.99/week or $29.99 lifetime (journeybot, 2026)
competitors.note: The enthusiast/onebag app — group packing plus per-item weight tracking, which nobody else does well and which the ultralight crowd genuinely wants. The soft spot is naked: iCloud sync across your own devices requires Pro, 'where several other apps include sync for free.' A $3.99/week ask — $207/yr annualised — for a packing checklist is the single most quotable price in this category, and it is the price of the feature that just means 'my phone and my iPad show the same list.'

competitors.name: TripList (AI packing checklist, 2025 rebuild)
competitors.model: Free for exactly one trip. Premium Weekly $2.99 or Premium Yearly $19.99 (iOS App Store IAP list). Its own listing: 'One trip is free. Creating more than one trip is a paid feature and requires a Premium subscription.'
competitors.note: The new AI wave, and the most instructive competitor because it markets on our exact promise while metering harder than anyone: the store copy says 'Offline & Private — no account, no ads, no data sync' and the privacy card still declares collection of User ID, Device ID, product interaction and crash data. Only 4.1 from 7 ratings, so it has no moat yet. Early reviewers asked for the basics — 'Ability to edit anything from titles to entries', 'Ability to clone a list', sorting, and per-item notes — which is a free feature spec for us. Note also the older TripList (last updated 2017, listed on AlternativeTo as 'Abandoned by the developer') capped free users at a single trip and 25 items.

competitors.name: Packing Pro (Quinn Genzel)
competitors.model: $2.99 one-time, no subscription (Her Packing List, TooManyAdapters)
competitors.note: The old-guard power tool and the only mainstream app that handles a whole household — lists for children, babies, adults and pets, with an 'expert' assistant that generates for multiple people, plus real export. Two fatal gaps: iOS only, and its last App Store update was May 2022, so it predates on-device AI and live weather. Reviewers' standing criticism is 'intensive set up' — it is a database you must feed before it repays you. Our opening is the opposite end: usable list in one tap, deepen later.

competitors.name: Wanderlog (packing checklist inside a trip planner)
competitors.model: Free tier is genuinely generous — unlimited trips, collaboration, checklists. Pro $39.99–$59.99/yr (commonly quoted as $49/yr) buys offline access, Gmail scanning, route optimisation, flight alerts.
competitors.note: The real threat is bundling: if someone already planned the trip here, they will not open a second app to pack. Packing lists are free in the base app and collaboration is free, which neutralises our sharing edge for that user. Two openings. First, the packing list is a minor feature of a heavy product — reviewers' #1 complaint is that it 'feels slow and laggy, especially on mobile or when the itinerary gets big', plus 'occasional server downtime or sync issues' and advice to download backups before travelling. Second, offline access is a Pro feature, so the free user's checklist can fail at the gate. An account is required.

competitors.name: The free printable PDF checklist (Passion Planner, Travel Fashion Girl, Maple Planners, PrintBlame's 16 variants, Day Designer, plus Gumroad/TPT-style paid family lists)
competitors.model: Free — very often in exchange for an email address; some are paid downloads on Gumroad
competitors.note: This is what most people actually use, and it is our closest functional competitor, not the funded app. It wins on being instantly understandable, printable, and dead on a kitchen counter where you will see it. It loses on being uneditable and unshareable. Its worst behaviour is the email wall: sites gate the PDF behind a newsletter signup, and the recurring complaint is that the file never arrives — users describe being 'led in circles' after subscribing and the sites continuing to demand signup after verification. Note that at least one site (tracabout.com) now advertises 'no email required' as the differentiator, which tells you how sore the point is.

competitors.name: Apple Reminders / Notes, Google Keep, and the reused spreadsheet
competitors.model: Free, pre-installed, already synced, already trusted
competitors.note: The silent majority. Google Keep shows up in every 'best apps for travel packing' listicle alongside the purpose-built apps, which is the tell: people duplicate last year's note and edit it. It wins on zero adoption cost and on being where their other lists already are. It loses on three specific things we can beat: no trip-type starting content (you type 'toothbrush' from memory every time, which is precisely how things get forgotten), no packed/total progress, and sharing that drags the other person into an account. Our whole design job against this competitor is to be faster than duplicating a note — first useful list in one tap, no signup, no app install.

complaints.complaint: It crashes or loses your progress in the middle of packing, and reinstalling wipes the templates you built. The review is titled 'Buggy when you need it' and reports crashes during use, loss of packed-item progress, TripIt sync problems, and custom templates gone after a reinstall.
complaints.source: PackPoint, iOS App Store review by 'Itinerant Teacher', 08/30/2025 (read via the App Store reviews page)
complaints.weWinIf: We already persist on every single mutation — app.js save() runs after every check, add and delete, so there is no 'unsaved' state to lose. But we have the other half of this failure and no answer to it: clear the browser, switch phones, or hit an iOS storage eviction and localStorage is gone with no copy anywhere. Ship 'Download list (.txt)' and 'Open a saved list' next to the existing Copy link / QR / Print row in index.html:1254-1257. That is our reinstall story, and it is one function next to helpers.js encodeList.

complaints.complaint: The customisation you paid for does not carry forward: 'The paid version enable customization which is awesome, but it doesn't carry forward to the next trip/list' — and a separate reviewer wishes 'they had customer support to help fix the issue.'
complaints.source: PackPoint, Google Play review text surfaced via search snippet — the Play page itself would not render for direct verification, so treat the wording as closely-quoted rather than certified verbatim
complaints.weWinIf: This is the strongest gap in our build, not just theirs. app.js:36 uses a single key, `const KEY = 'packing-list'`, holding one `{name, items}` object, so we support exactly one trip at a time and 'Uncheck all (reuse trip)' (index.html:1254) is the entire reuse story — it preserves the list but destroys the record of the trip you just took. Move to `packing-list.trips` keyed by id, with a trip switcher at the top and a 'Duplicate this trip' action. Reuse is the category's unsolved problem and it is pure local-storage work for us.

complaints.complaint: Nothing is editable after you create the trip: 'once a trip or city is entered, it cannot be modified — only deleted and recreated from scratch', and 'You can't change the dates once you have included them which is a bummer because you have to create a new list from the beginning.'
complaints.source: PackPoint, iOS App Store 2-star review 'Limited options' by 'S. Frequent flyers', 02/11/2025; and thoughtcard.com PackPoint review
complaints.weWinIf: Everything editable in place, and no regeneration step that can eat your edits. We are half-right: the trip name is live-editable (app.js `tripName` input listener) but item labels are not — app.js only offers addCustom and a splice delete, so a typo means delete and retype. Make the item label a click-to-edit field, and make presets purely additive forever (helpers.js mergePreset already is — that is the right instinct, keep it).

complaints.complaint: The app demands a destination it does not have. 'The app requires a location but lacks many common cities — Maui and Kona, for example, aren't even included.'
complaints.source: PackPoint, iOS App Store 2-star review 'Limited options', 02/11/2025
complaints.weWinIf: We require nothing. There is no city lookup, no date picker, no mandatory field — index.html:1235 is a free-text trip name with a placeholder, and it is optional. That is a genuine feature and it currently reads as an absence. Say it in the empty state: 'No destination to look up, no dates to enter. Tap a preset.'

complaints.complaint: The list is built in the cloud, so you need a connection to create one — in an app whose entire audience is about to be on a plane or abroad without data.
complaints.source: journeybot.app 2026 packing-app comparison, stated as PackPoint's core limitation
complaints.weWinIf: sw.js caches the app and everything runs from localStorage, so we work in airplane mode with the radio off. This is our single biggest hard advantage and it is currently claimed only in the footer colophon ('no account, no ads'), which the portfolio brief says nobody reads as grey body copy. This app has no `.trust` block at all — add one, and word it as the negative claim: 'Turn the wifi off. It still works. Nothing about this list leaves your phone.'

complaints.complaint: Multi-stop and multi-climate trips are unsupported: the app cannot consolidate a multi-destination itinerary into one packing plan 'without creating a bunch of mini trips.'
complaints.source: PackPoint, iOS App Store review by 'farbeyondme', 04/03/2025 (developer response acknowledges the limitation)
complaints.weWinIf: Our additive presets already solve this and nobody has noticed: tapping Beach then Winter then International composes one list and adds only what is missing (helpers.js mergePreset, case-insensitive dedupe). Surface it — after a second preset, the toast should say '7 items added — Beach + Winter now in one list' instead of the current bare count. One list for a five-country trip is a headline, not a footnote.

complaints.complaint: You cannot pack for a family. PackPoint 'can only be used for one person' and offers no way to add travellers or see everything in one place; on Packr, family mode is behind Premium.
complaints.source: toomanyadapters.com best-packing-apps roundup (PackPoint cons); herpackinglist.com roundup ('Can only be used for one person'); Packr feature/pricing pages
complaints.weWinIf: Two moves, both free for us. First, an optional per-item owner tag ('Mia', 'Sam') with a filter, so one list covers the household but each person can see only theirs. Second — the thing no competitor can copy — the existing share link already hands a whole list to another phone with no account on either end (helpers.js encodeList, app.js shareBtn/qrBtn). The hint copy at index.html:1302 already says 'send it to whoever's packing the kids' bags'; that sentence is the strategy and deserves to be a button label, not a hint.

complaints.complaint: Ads and paywall pressure inside the packing workflow itself, on a tool that used to be free: 'aggressive paywall transitions force users to pay for basic functionality that was previously free' and 'recent attraction-based ads are obstructive to the packing workflow', alongside data-loss reports after an update.
complaints.source: marlvel.ai aggregated review analysis for Packr (com.jeremieleroy.packr). This is a third-party summary of recent reviews, not a verbatim user quote — flagged as such rather than dressed up
complaints.weWinIf: Zero ad surface, and the portfolio's hard rule applies with full force here: nothing over the list, nothing in the thumb zone that moves or grows. Our tip jar is a header link (index.html:1229) — keep it a link, never a button, and never anywhere near the checkbox column, which is where a half-awake person's thumb lands at 6am.

complaints.complaint: Subscription pricing for a checklist. TripList: 'One trip is free. Creating more than one trip is a paid feature' — Premium Weekly $2.99 or Yearly $19.99. PackGoat: Pro at $3.99/week. Packr: ten separate IAP price points up to $49.99.
complaints.source: iOS App Store IAP listings for TripList (id6745196831) and Packr (id1208312901); journeybot 2026 comparison for PackGoat
complaints.weWinIf: Unlimited trips, unlimited items, no counter, no card field anywhere in the DOM. Put the comparison where competitors put their pricing table: 'Trips: unlimited. Items: unlimited. Price: none.' A person who just hit 'you've used your one free trip' should be able to confirm in three seconds that it cannot happen here.

complaints.complaint: Sync between your own two devices is a paid feature — PackGoat's iCloud sync 'requires PackGoat Pro, where several other apps include sync for free' — and on Packr the app 'asks you to sign in with your Apple account before trips will save and sync.'
complaints.weWinIf: Our answer to sync is the QR code, and it is better than it looks: phone-to-phone, no account, no cloud, works across ecosystems. But app.js showQr() calls qrcode(0,'M') with auto version selection and simply toasts 'Could not draw the QR' when the payload is too big — a 60-item list with long labels will hit that wall, silently, at the worst moment. Cap it gracefully (drop to error-correction 'L', and if it still will not fit, say 'too long for a QR — use Copy link' rather than 'Could not draw'). Same class of bug in helpers.js decodeList, which silently truncates a shared list at 300 items.

complaints.complaint: You cannot reorder items, and long generated lists become unmanageable — reviewers cite the inability to reorder alongside interface inefficiencies like 'entering dates one field at a time instead of using a calendar selector.'
complaints.source: PackPoint review summaries on justuseapp.com (the page itself 403'd on direct fetch, so this is from the search-engine summary of that page) plus an iOS 4-star review dated 01/30/2020 for the date-entry quote
complaints.weWinIf: index.html:1244 renders one flat `<ul id="list">` in insertion order with no grouping, no sort and no filter — so a merged Essentials + Camping + Winter list is 26 unsorted rows and we inherit exactly this complaint at scale. Ship two cheap things before drag-and-drop: category grouping (helpers.js PRESETS are flat string arrays today — retag them as `{label, cat}` and the sections come free) and a 'Hide packed' toggle so the remaining items rise to the top as you work.

complaints.complaint: Deleting is instant and irreversible. This one is ours, not a competitor's.
complaints.source: Our own code — app.js:82, the `.x` button splices the item and re-renders with no confirmation and no undo
complaints.weWinIf: The studio base CSS already ships an undo affordance inside the toast (index.html:781, `#toast .undo`) and this app never uses it. Wire delete to a toast with Undo. Same for the shared-link import at app.js init(), which currently uses a blocking native `confirm()` to ask before replacing the user's list — replace it with an in-page choice that also offers 'Merge into my list', since mergePreset already proves we can merge without duplicating.

complaints.complaint: The free printable is not free: sites gate the PDF behind a newsletter signup and users report the file never arrives — being 'led in circles' after subscribing, and sites continuing to demand signup after the email was verified.
complaints.source: Search-snippet synthesis across free-printable-packing-list blog pages and their comment threads; no single identifiable thread could be opened and verified, so treat this as directionally real but unverified. Corroborating signal: tracabout.com markets its list specifically as requiring no email
complaints.weWinIf: Print is already a first-class button (index.html:1257) with real print CSS that strips the chrome and prints black checkboxes. We beat the printable competitor on their own turf — editable, no email, no watermark, and reprintable next year. Make the print output look designed: trip name as a heading, items grouped, and a footer line that is the URL of the tool rather than a logo.

complaints.complaint: Open scepticism that the category deserves money at all: the app 'isn't worth spending your money on as anyone with a brain can list what they need for a holiday or work trip.'
complaints.source: PackPoint, Google Play review surfaced via search snippet (Play page would not render for direct verification)
complaints.weWinIf: This reviewer is our user, not our critic. The argument only works against paid apps — nothing has to be justified when nothing is charged and nothing is installed. Design for the sceptic's path: land on the page, tap one preset, have a usable list in under three seconds, with no onboarding, no permission prompt and no 'create your first trip' wall (the wall PackPoint reviewers describe as 'no way out until they create a list').

tableStakes: Multiple saved trips. Every competitor including the abandoned ones has this; TripList charges $19.99/yr for it. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — app.js:36 `const KEY = 'packing-list'` stores exactly one `{name, items}` object, and index.html:1254 'Uncheck all (reuse trip)' is the substitute. Starting a second trip means overwriting the first.

Categories/sections (documents, toiletries, clothes, electronics). WE DO NOT HAVE IT — helpers.js PRESETS are flat arrays of strings and index.html:1244 is a single flat `<ul id="list">`. Tapping three presets produces ~26 ungrouped rows.
Quantities per item ('5 × socks'). WE DO NOT HAVE IT — helpers.js addCustom stores only `{label, done}`; a user has to type 'Socks ×5' into the label by hand.

Trip length as an input, driving quantities. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — there is no date, nights or duration field anywhere in index.html. The app's own portfolio description promises 'weather and duration'; the build delivers trip type only. Either build a nights field or stop claiming duration.

Weather-aware suggestions. WE DO NOT HAVE IT and should not — a forecast means a network call and an API key, which breaks the offline and no-tracking promise. The Beach/Winter presets are the manual stand-in. This must be stated in-product as a deliberate trade, not left as a silent hole a reviewer will find.

Edit an item's text after adding it. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — app.js supports add (addCustom) and splice-delete only. A typo costs a delete and a retype, and this is the exact complaint reviewers filed against TripList ('Ability to edit anything from titles to entries').
Undo a delete. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — app.js:82 splices immediately on tap. Notably the studio base already ships the component: index.html:781 styles `#toast .undo`, and this app never renders it.
Reorder items, or at least sort/filter a long list. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — renderList paints strict insertion order, with no drag, no sort and no 'hide packed' toggle.

Multiple travellers / per-person lists. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — one flat list. Partially mitigated by the share link handing a separate copy to another phone (app.js shareBtn), which is arguably better, but there is no in-list owner tag.

Export or back up the list as a file. WE DO NOT HAVE IT — sharing is URL-hash only (helpers.js encodeList) plus print. helpers.js decodeList silently truncates at 300 items, and app.js showQr fails with a bare 'Could not draw the QR' once the payload exceeds QR capacity. Clearing site data destroys the only copy.

Works offline with no account, and print. WE HAVE BOTH — sw.js caches the app, everything lives in localStorage, and index.html carries real print CSS plus a Print button (index.html:1257). This is where we beat PackPoint (cloud-generated lists) and Wanderlog (offline is a $49/yr Pro feature).

A visible privacy/trust stamp rather than a claim in body copy. WEAK — the only statement is the footer colophon 'On your device, in your pocket, at the airport — no account, no ads'. There is no `.trust` component in index.html's body, so the portfolio's strongest asset is stated in the smallest type on the page.
differentiators: Airplane-mode proof, and prove it out loud. PackPoint builds its list in the cloud; Wanderlog charges $49/yr for offline. Ours is a cached static page over localStorage. The line to run is a dare, not a disclaimer: 'Turn the wifi off. It still works.'

Presets that compose instead of replace. helpers.js mergePreset adds only what is missing, case-insensitively, so Beach + With kids + International is one coherent list. This is the direct answer to PackPoint's acknowledged multi-stop failure ('a bunch of mini trips') and to every app that regenerates and eats your edits.

Handing a list to another person costs nothing on either end. Link plus QR (app.js shareBtn/qrBtn, helpers.js encodeList) moves the whole list phone-to-phone with no account, no install and no ecosystem — while Packr's family mode is premium and PackGoat charges $3.99/week for sync between your own two devices. Recipients' checkboxes start fresh, which is exactly right for 'you pack the kids' bags, I'll do ours.'

The trip is reusable, which is the category's unsolved problem. 'It doesn't carry forward to the next trip' is the most-repeated complaint we found. 'Uncheck all (reuse trip)' is already the right instinct; upgraded into saved, duplicable trips it becomes the reason to choose us.

A printable that is genuinely free. The blog printables want an email and often do not deliver the file; we print an edited, personalised, grouped checklist with no signup, no watermark and no download folder — for the person who tapes it inside the suitcase lid.

Nothing to set up and nothing to justify. Packing Pro's standing criticism is 'intensive set up'; PackPoint traps people in a creation screen 'with no way out until they create a list'. Our target is a usable list within one tap of landing, no onboarding, no permission prompt, no first-run wall.

Honesty as a feature where we are weaker. We cannot fetch a forecast without breaking the privacy promise, so the presets carry the weather knowledge and we say why in plain words. A stated trade-off reads as confidence; a silent omission reads as a missing feature.

Legibility and one-handed operation as a design commitment, not an accessibility footnote. sws-prefs.js already gives text size, density, contrast and a real dark mode — which matters at 5am in a dim hallway far more than it does at a desk.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: In 2026 the category has split in two. The classic planners (PackPoint, Packr, Packing Pro) look like 2017 iOS: sky-blue-to-teal gradients, a cartoon suitcase or aeroplane mark, emoji category headers, five-icon tab bars, and a weather card pinned to the top. The new wave (journeybot, TripList AI, Packify, JetPach) is AI-forward: a generation prompt as the hero, shimmering 'thinking' states, soft violet accents, and privacy language borrowed from Apple ('on-device', 'no account') printed straight on the store listing. What reads as dated in 2026: glossy sky-blue gradients, skeuomorphic luggage illustration, a globe or aeroplane in the logo, tab bars, and any hero image of a beach. What reads as current: a single scrolling column, category-grouped checklists with a sticky progress bar, generous rounded tap targets, system typography, a restrained single accent, real dark mode, and — new this cycle, driven by the AI apps — explicit privacy statements treated as design elements rather than legal text. Our advantage is that we can make the privacy claim as an object because it is actually true, while they print it beside a data-collection disclosure.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: This app is opened in exactly three states, none of them calm. Eleven at night before an early flight, half-packed, tired, mildly anxious that something is being forgotten. Six in the morning at the front door or in the back of a taxi, one hand on a suitcase handle or a child, phone battery already down, checking the last four items. And on the return leg in a hotel room, trying to make sure nothing is left in the bathroom. Airport and hotel wifi is bad, roaming data may be off, and the person may be standing up. That dictates everything: no network call on any critical path; progress visible without scrolling; checkbox targets big enough for a thumb on a moving train; nothing that animates, grows or overlays near the thumb zone; every destructive action undoable, because a mis-tap while walking is not a decision; and a dark mode dark enough for a hallway at 5am. It also dictates tone — this user does not need cheerfulness, they need certainty. The emotional payoff the design should build toward is one specific moment: the list going fully green at the front door.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: calm, deep, dependable, luggage-tag practical, one-handed, unhurried, quietly confident, no cheerleading

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Keep the teal family but move it from 'travel-app cyan' to deep petrol/marine ink — hue ≈192, chroma ≈0.10 with a markedly darker accent value than today, cool paper, a 'band' texture reading as a boarding-pass or luggage-tag stripe, and radius pulled back from 16 to ~12. Pair it with a warm amber support at hue ≈28 used for exactly one job: the still-to-pack state, so the page resolves from amber to deep teal as the list completes. Concretely, an accent around oklch(0.44 0.10 192) in light and its lifted counterpart in dark, against a cool-tinted canvas.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Two collisions have to be solved, and the sharper one is internal. skins.mjs currently gives packing-list hue 188 / chroma 0.12 / paper cool / voice plain / texture none / r16 — and grocery-list hue 158 / chroma 0.14 / paper cool / voice plain / texture none / r16. Those two share four of the five identity axes and sit 30° apart on the fifth. They are also functionally identical products: a tappable checklist you work one-handed while holding something. Right now they will read as the same app in two tints, which is the exact failure mode the skins file was written to prevent. Hue alone cannot fix it, so the fix is value, chroma and texture: grocery-list is a bright, mid-light, vivid grass green with a friendly 1.06 scale — supermarket daylight. Packing-list should be its opposite in register: darker, more muted, cooler, with a graphic band and tighter corners. Night-before-the-flight, not Tuesday-afternoon-shopping. The second collision is scan-to-pdf at hue 202 / chroma 0.12 / cool — only 14° away and identical chroma today; dropping our chroma to 0.10 and going deeper in value separates on saturation and lightness, while scan-to-pdf keeps its grid texture and technical voice against our band and plain voice. Nudging 188 to 192 buys a little more distance from grocery-list without wandering into scan-to-pdf's cyan. Against the category, deep petrol teal is the right answer for a different reason: every competitor in the space is a light sky-blue-to-teal gradient, so going darker and more muted in the same hue family reads as the grown-up version of a familiar thing rather than another entry in the pile — recognisably 'travel' at a glance for the 6am user, but visibly not another cartoon-suitcase app. The amber support earns its place semantically: it is the only colour that appears on unfinished items, so completion is legible peripherally, and it echoes the tag-and-stamp language of luggage without any illustration.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Do not stay at a light, bright cyan-teal — that is both the category cliché and the thing that makes us look like grocery-list. Do not drift green (toward 158/142, grocery-list and qr-maker) or drift into 200-206 cyan (scan-to-pdf, and signup-sheets' 200 support). Do not switch to warm/cream paper: sub-plans (174, warm) sits 14° away and would become a near-twin, and moving-boxes (72, warm, kraft) already owns the warm-paper slot inside this same Moving & Travel hub. Avoid the beach palette entirely — turquoise plus coral plus sand is what every competitor's App Store screenshot already looks like, and it makes a business-trip or funeral-travel list feel wrong. No gradients, no aeroplane or globe motif, no palm-tree or suitcase illustration. And no green-for-done / red-for-missing pairing: the completion state should be the accent itself deepening, so the signal survives colour-blindness and the dark hallway.

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH. Verified directly by fetching the source page: PackPoint's iOS rating (4.7 / ~2,400) and its in-app purchase prices ($2.99 / $0.99 / $0.99); the PackPoint critical reviews quoted with usernames and dates ('Itinerant Teacher' 08/30/2025, 'S.
